inhibition activity of lipid accumulation in oleic acid-induced HepG2 cells

Abstract
Two acid polysaccharides were obtained from steamed ginseng (GPS-1 and GPS -2)
through water extraction, ion-exchange chromatography and gel chromatography. The
structural features and ability of the polysaccharides to inhibit lipid accumulation in
oleic acid -induced HepG2 cells were studied. GPS-1 consisted of type I
arabinogalactans (AG -I), arabinogalactans-II (AG-II) and rhamnogalacturonan I
(RG-I) domains. GPS-2 was a pectin -like polysaccharide consisting mainly of the
homogalacturonan (HG) domain and a small amount of AG domain. Both GPS-1 and
GPS-2 had branches attaching on O-3 of (1 →6)-GalA or O-4 of (1 →2)-Rha and
terminated by either Ara or Gal. An in vitro experiment revealed that GPS-1 treatment
at 50–400 μg/ml could dose-dependently decrease intracellular lipid accumulation and
cholesterol (TC) and triglycerides ( TG) levels. GPS -1 exerted a more serious
hypolipidemic effect than GPS -2 did. Moreover, GP S-1 considerably increased the
phosphorylation of AMP -activated protein kinase (AMPK) and affect ed the
expression of AMPK downstream targets, including the inhibition of the protein
expression of sterol regulatory element-binding protein 1c (SREBP-1c) and activation
of Acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC). Results suggest that GPS -1 could inhibit lipid
accumulation via the AMPK the signalling pathway.
Keywords: steamed ginseng; pectin; lipid accumulation; HepG2 cell

1. Introduction
Diabetes is an endocrine metabolic disease that causes glucose, fat and protein
Journal Pre-proof

Journal Pre-proof
3

metabolism disorders due to the insufficient production of or reduced sensitivity to
insulin in the body; it is the greatest threat to human health today [1]. For a long time,
people understood diabetes as a disorder in glucose metabolism, and its treatment
measures focus ed on controlling blood sugar. In 2001, McGarry reported that lipid
metabolic disorder is the root of metabolism disorders in type 2 diabetes [2]. As a
primary o r secondary disease, lipid metabolic disorders are closely related to the
occurrence, development and prognosis of major diseases of the entire body [3].
Therefore, lipid metabolism regulation plays an important role in the prevention and
treatment of type 2 diabetes mellitus and its complications.
Commonly used hypoglycemic blood -regulating drugs have side effects [4-5].
Therefore, an increasing number of researchers have focused on identifying active
substances from natural products to prevent abnormal glycolipid metabolism.
Amongst these substances, plant polysaccharides could be used for the development
of new hypoglycemic and lipid -lowering drugs because they are non -toxic and have
no side effects.
Panax ginseng C.A. Meyer, which belongs to the family Araliaceae, is a popular
medicinal plant, and many studies have proven that ginseng contains various active
components ( e.g. ginsenoside and polysaccharides), which play an important
promotion and protection roles in blood sugar reduction, improvement of lipid
metabolism disorder, insulin sensitivity enhancement, adipocyte differentiation and so
on [6-9]. Polysaccharides, one of the main active components of ginseng, also help in
the prevention and treatment of diabetes. Niu et al. found that ginseng polysaccharide
Journal Pre-proof

Journal Pre-proof
4

plays a hypoglycemic role by affecting purine, tryptophan and fatty acid metabolism
and other metabolic processes in diabetic rats [10]. Sun et al. confirmed that the acid
polysaccharides of ginseng are the main hypoglycemic components of ginseng
polysaccharides, which can reduce glucose by decreasing oxidative stress and
stimulating insulin secretion [11]. Our previous study showed that the acid
polysaccharide of steamed ginseng (GP S, steamed at 120 °C) has better
antihyperglycemic activity than that of white ginseng. Moreover, GPS reduces blood
sugar, improves antioxidant systems, and enhances blood lipids in diabetic mice [12].
However, the antidiabetic mechanism of GPS and the structural basis of its
antidiabetic effect are unclear. In addition, GPS is composed of two different fractions,
namely, GPS-1 and GPS -2. The biological activities of polysaccharides as complex
biomolecules are closely related to their structure properties. T hus, structural
identification of polysaccharide s is essential in understanding the mechanism of
physiological activities and the effects of the structure–activity relationship. Therefore,
we investigated the structural features of GPS -1 and G PS-2 and used oleic acid
induction to establish a hepatocellular model of lipid accumulation . The purpose was
to determine the effect on lipid metabolism and the possible molecular mechanism.

2. Materials and Methods
2.1. Preparation of streamed ginseng and pectic polysaccharides
Panax ginseng roots aged five years were collected from Changbai Mountain,
Jilin Province, China , in August 2018. Steamed ginseng and pectin polysaccharides
Journal Pre-proof

Journal Pre-proof
5

were prepared in accordance with our previous report . In brief, fresh ginseng roots
were washed and wrapped with clean gauze. The fresh ginseng was steamed at 120 °C
for 3 h and dried at 50 °C until the moisture content was 14%. The acid
polysaccharides, GPS-1 and GPS -2, were obtained through water extraction, ethanol
precipitation, ion -exchange chromatography (DEAE -cellulose column, 7.0×30 cm)
and gel chromatography (Sephadex G-100 column, 2.5×100 cm). High-performance
liquid chromatography (HPLC; equipped with a TSK -G3000 PWXL column) revealed
that GPS-1 and GPS -2 had a single symmetric peak and molecular weight s of
9.61×105 and 3.39×105 Da, respectively [12].

2.2. General methods
The content of uronic acid was determined with the M-hydroxybiphenyl method,
and the reference was GalA [13]. The monosaccharide composition of
polysaccharides was analysed through a combination of PMP derivation and HPLC as
described by D. Wang et al. [14]. In brief , the polysaccharides (2 mg) w ere
hydrolysed with 0.5 ml of methanol solution containing 1 M hydrochloric acid at
80 °C for 16 h . The hydrate was further hydrolysed for 1 h by using 2 M TFA at
120 °C. The hydrolysed product was derived with 1 -phenyl-3-methyl-5-pyrazolone
(PMP) agent. The resulting derivate was detected by HPLC using an UlitiMate3000
instrument (ThermoFinningan, San Jose, CA, USA) equipped with a DIKMA Inertsil
ODS-3 column (46 mm×150 mm, 5 μm, Dikma, Japan). The column temperature was
maintained at 25 °C. The mobile phase was composed of 82.0% phosphate-buffered
Journal Pre-proof

Journal Pre-proof
6

saline (PBS, 0.1 M, pH 7.0) and 18.0% acetonitrile (v/v) with a flow rate of 1.0
ml/min and detected at 245 nm. The injection volume of the PMP derivate was 20 μL.

2.3. Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy
GPS-1 and GP S-2 (2 mg each) were dried, homogenised with KBr tablets and
subjected to Fourier transform infrared spectroscopy ( FT-IR). The recorded values
ranged from 400 cm-1 to 4000 cm-1.

2.4. Carboxyl group reduction
Samples (60 mg) dissolved in 55 ml of distilled water and
1-cyclohexyl-3-(2-morpholinoethyl) carbodiimidemetho -p-toluenesulphonate (CMC,
60 mg) was added. The PH value of the resulting solution was adjusted to 4.75 by
using 0.01 M HCl and maintained for 3 h. Then, 2 M KBH 4 (30 ml) and 4 M HCl
were added to the solution to keep the PH value of the solution at 7. The resulting
solution was dialysed against distilled water for th ree days, lyophilised and subjected
to monosaccharide analysis [15].

2.5. Methylation analysis
Polysaccharide samples (1 mg) were dried, dissolved in DMSO (0.2 ml) and
stirred at room temperature for 12 h. DMSO–NaOH solution (0.2 ml) solution was
added to the resulting solution and stirred for 10 min. Then, methyl iodide was added
and stirred for 40 min, and 2 ml of distilled water was added to terminate the reaction.
Journal Pre-proof

Journal Pre-proof
7

The methylated polysaccharide was extracted with dichloromethane, dried with
nitrogen and detected via FT-IR analysis to determine if the methylation was complete.
Afterwards, the methylated sample was hydrolysed by 2 M TFA (1 ml) at 120 °C for 2
h, reduced with NaBH 4 (10 mg/ml) overnight and subjected to acetylation with acetic
anhydride in accordance with a method in literature [16]. The resulting alditol acetates
were detected through gas chromatography–mass spectrometry (GC-MS) using a TSQ
8000 instrument (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA) equipped with a TG -5SiLMS
column (30 m×0.25 mm×0.25 μm). The column temperature was maintained at
120 °C for 2 min and subsequently increased to 280 °C for 5 min at a rate of 10 °C
/min; then it was maintained for 2 min. Data were acquired within 30–400 m/z.

2.6. Cell line culture
HepG2 cells were cultured in DMEM medium containing 10 % FBS at 37 °C in a
humidified incubator with and 5% CO2. When the cell density reached 80%–90%, the
cells were digested with 0.25% trypsin and passaged in a 1:3 ratio. The logarithmic
cells were used in the experiment.

2.7. Cytotoxicity assay
The in vitro cellular toxicity of the polysaccharides was investigated via CCK8
assay [17]. In brief, a HepG2 cell suspension (1 × 10 5 cells/ml) was inoculated onto
96-well cell culture plates at 100 μl per hole. After 24 h, the original culture medium
was sucked out , and different concentrations of samples solution were added to each
Journal Pre-proof

Journal Pre-proof
8

well at a concentration of 0 –800 μg/ml. The total volume of each hole was 200 μl.
After mixing, it was cultured at 37 °C for 72 h. Four hours before the end of culturing,
10 μl CCK8 was added to each hole , and the OD value at 4 50 nm was determined
using an ELISA reader (TECAN GENios, Switzerland).

2.8. Induction of lipid accumulation in HepG2 cells and drug treatment
HepG2 cells (5×105 cells/mL) were inoculated into 12-well cell culture plates (1
ml/well). When the cells were confluent to 10% –80%, the culture medium was
replaced with a serum-free medium for 12 h, and 200 μM oleic acid was added to
induce lipid accumulation in the cells. The cells were incubated with GPS-1 and
GPS-2 at different concentrations (50, 100, 200 and 400 μg/ml) for 12 h and/or 24 h at
37 °C. Metformin (2 mM) was used as positive control.

2.9. Determination of triglyceride and total cholesterol levels
An oleic acid -induced HepG2 cell model w as established and culture d with
different concentrations of GPS -1 and GPS -2 and metformin for 12 and 24 h,
respectively, as described above. At the end of the culturing, the cells were washed
with PBS, fully lysed with cell lysate and centrifuged. The supernatant was collected,
and the levels of total cholesterol (TC) and triglyceride ( TG) were detected using
commercial reagent kits according to the manufacturer’s instructions (Nanjing
Jiancheng Bioengineering Institute, Nanjing, China).

Journal Pre-proof

Journal Pre-proof
9

2.10. Oil red O staining
HepG2 (5×105 cells/ml) was inoculated on a six -well plate with a clean cover slip
and induced with oleic acid for 24 h as described above . The control group was
treated with DMEM medium, the positive group was treated with 2 mM metformin
and the polysaccharide group was treated with different concentrations of GP S-1 and
GPS-2 (50–400 μg/ml). Each group of cells was incubated at 37 °C for 24 h, washed
with PBS three times, fixed with 10% formalin for 40 min at room temperature ,
rewashed with PBS and stained using an oil red O working solution for 20 min at
room temperature . The staining results were observed under a microscope. After
observation, 0.5 ml of 60% isopropanol solution was added and maintained for 15
min, and the absorbance value was determined at 485 nm [18].
The cells were washed twice with PBS buffer and mixed with 75% ethanol for 10
min. Then, the cells were incubated with 0.5 % oil red O working solution for 30 min.
Afterwards, that the cells were further washed with PBS buffer. Exactly 500 μl
isopropanol (100%) was added after the water was completely removed . Finally, the
cells were incubated for 10 min and injected onto a 96-well plate, the absorbance of
each well was determined at 510 nm [19].

2.11. Western blot analysis
The total protein was extracted from the HepG2 cells. The protein concentration of
the cell homogenates was determined using a BCA kit (Solarbio Life Sciences, China).
An equal amount of protein (50 μg) was subjected to SDS-PAGE transferred onto a
Journal Pre-proof

Journal Pre-proof
10

PVDF membrane via the wet membrane transfer method. Then, the membrane was
blocked with 5% BSA at room temperature for 2 h and incubated with AMPK,
p-AMPK, p-ACC, SREBP -1c and β-actin at 4 °C overnight. After washing the
membrane with TBST three times, it was incubated with the secondary antibody for 1
h, washed three times, and added with a chemiluminescent HRP substrate reagent
(Millipore Corporation, Billerica, USA) to visualise the target proteins . The grey
values were analysed using Image J software.

2.12. Statistical analysis
The results were expressed as mean ± standard deviation ( SD). The statistical
significance of the differences between groups was evaluated using ANOV A followed
by Student’s t-test. The significant differences of data were displayed as follows: p <
0.05 is signified by *, and p < 0.01 is signified by **.

3. Results and Discussion
3.1 Characterisation of GPS-1and GPS-2
GPS-1 and GPS -2 were reduced with CMC, and the reduced product s (GPS-1R
and GPS-2R) were subjected to monosaccharide and FT-IR analysis to further analyse
the glycoside bond types of the two polysaccharides . According to the
monosaccharide results (Fig 1B and Table 1), GPS -1R contained three
monosaccharides, namely, Rha, Gal and Ara with a molar ratio of 1.00: 6.77:3.41, and
a trace amount of Glc (<1.0%). After reduction, the content of Gal increased by 11.41%
Journal Pre-proof

Journal Pre-proof
11

compared with that in GPS-1 (Fig 1A and Table 1). The increase in Gal in GPS -1R
was a result of GalA reduction . The results also indicated that GPS -1 was an acid
heteropolysaccharide dominated by arabinogalactose. GPS-2R was composed mainly
of Gal (8 6.02%) with small amounts of Rha (3.21%), Glc ( 3.43%) and Ara (7.34%).
The Gal content in GPS -2R (86.02%) was nearly 6 7% higher than that in GPS -2
(19.23%) (Fig 1C, 2D and Table 1), indicating that GPS -2 was a homogalacturonan
(HG)-rich pectin. No GalA was detected in GPS -1R, showing that GalA was reduced
completely. By contrast, trace amount of GalA in GPS-2 was still detected; it was
probably related to the high content of GalA and could not be reduced completely by
two reduction processes.
Immediately afterwards, the four polysaccharides were analysed by FT -IR. As
shown in Fig. 2, the intense absorption bands at 3401–3422 cm−1 in the FT-IR spectra
corresponded to O-H stretching vibration [20]. The signals at 2929.81–2934.64 cm−1
and 16 10.14–1645.33 cm−1 were assigned to C –H stretching vibration. The strong
absorptions at 1736.57 cm-1 for GPS-1 and 1736.51 cm-1 for GPS-2 were ascribed to
C=O stretching vibration of the carboxyl group [21]. Absorption peak s at 8 16.27–
823.12 cm−1 and 890.31–893.51 cm−1 were noted in the FT -IR spectra of GPS -1,
GPS-1R, GPS-2 and GPS -2R, respectively, indicating that the four polysaccharides
contained α and β configuration glycosidic bonds.
The partially methylated alditol acetates (PMAA) obtained from the
polysaccharide samples after methylation, hydrolysis, reduction, and acetylation were
analysed by GC -MS. The linkage type of sugar can be determined accurately
Journal Pre-proof

Journal Pre-proof
12

according to the peak order of the gas chromatography and the identification of the
main ion fragments of the mass spectrum. In addition, the proportion of this linkage
type in the polysaccharide repeat structure can be inferred according to the proportion
of different methylated monosaccharides [22-23]. Thus, the native and reduc ed
polysaccharides were converted into PMAAs and analysed by GC-MS. Their total ion
chromatogram (TIC) is shown in Fig. 3. The results showed that GPS -1 and GPS-1R
mainly contained seven glycosidic bond types, namely, t-Araf, 5 -Araf, t-Galp, 2 ,
4-Rha, 4-Galp, 4 -Glcp and 3, 6-Galp with molar ratio s of
1.67:2.62:1.30:1.00:6.23:0.77:1.07 for GPS -1 and
1.72:3.25:0.73:1.00:10.41:0.15:2.25 for GPS-2 respectively (Table 2). As reported by
Zhang et al ., ginseng pectin is mainly composed of three structural domains: type I
rhamnogalacturonan (RG-I), arabinogalactan (AG) and homogalacturonan (HG) [23].
RG-I is composed of multiple repeated 4)-α-D-GalpA (1→ 2)-α-L-Rhap (1→)
disaccharide units containing arabinogalactan (AG) in the side chain attached to the
backbone via C-4 of (1→2)-α-L-Rhap. Moreover, according to the glyosidic bonds of
β-D-Galp, AG can be divide d into AG -І and AG -Ⅱ. The former contains linear
(1→4)-β-D-Galp as the backbone . In comparison, AG -Ⅱ is composed of
β-(1→3)-D-Galp and β-(1→3, 6)-D-Galp with a high degree of branching [24].
According to the result, the content of (1→4) -Galp in GPS -1R increased by 10%
compared with that of GPS-1, indicating that the GalA contained in GPS -1 was
(1→4)-GalpA. Meanwhile, the presence of β -(1→4)-Galp and β-(1→3, 6)-Galp
suggested the existence of AG -І and AG -Ⅱ domains. The branches of GPS -1 was
Journal Pre-proof

Journal Pre-proof
13

located on O-4 of (1→2, 4)-linked Rha and O-3 of (1→3, 6) -linked Gal residues
(Table 2, Fig. 3A and 3B) and terminated with either Gal or Ara with the molar ratio
of 0.39:1.00. These results further confirm that GPS -1 contained RG-Ⅰ and AG
domains, which is consistent with the results of our previous study [11]. As shown in
Table 2 and Fig. 3C, the TIC profile of GPS-2 had seven peaks, which were identified
as t-Ara, 5 -Ara, t -Gal, 2,4 -Rha, 4 -Gal, 4 -Glc and 3,6 -Gal with a molar ratio of
2.13:3.31:1.34:1.00:4.07:2.67:2.71. After reduction, the content of 4 -Gal residue in
GPS-2R increased significantly ( 58.74%) compared with that of GPS -1, indicating
that GPS -2 is an acid heteropolysaccharide with α -(1→4)-GalpA as the main
structural unit. In addition, small amounts of t -Araf (2.41%), 5-Araf (3.86%), t-Galp
(3.31%), 2, 4 -Rhap (1.65%), 4 -Glcp (2.47%) and 3, 6-Galp (4.35%) were detected
(Table 2 and Fig. 3D). These results suggest that GPS -2 is a pectin -like
polysaccharide consisting mainly of the HG domain with a small amount of RG and
AG domains. GPS-2 also branched at O -4 position of 2, 4-linked Rha and O-3
position of 3, 6-linked Gal residues. The terminal of GPS-2 was composed of Gal and
Ara with a molar ratio of 1.80:1.00.
Pectin is a complex acid polysaccharide contained in ginseng . Zhang et al.
isolated two polysaccharides containing the RG-Ⅰ structural domain and four
polysaccharides containing the HG domain from white ginseng according to the
difference in charge; their structure s were characterised by 13C NMR analysis [24].
The RG -Ⅰ-containing polysac charides they obtained were composed of a small
content of GalA in the two domains and a large content of arabinans, galactans and/or
Journal Pre-proof

Journal Pre-proof
14

AG, which was similar to our results . However, the detailed glycosidic bond
information of the two RG -Ⅰ domains was not provided. Methylation analysis is an
important method to study the structure of polysaccharides; it is crucial in elucidating
the linkage type of monosaccharides and widely used to determine the connection
position of monosaccharide residues in oligosaccharides and polysaccharides [25]. In
this work, the carboxyl group of GPS -1 and GPS -2 was reduced and subjected to
methylation analysis to precisely determine the glycosidic bond type of the sample .
The results showed that GPS-1 and GPS -2 were composed of the same
monosaccharide residues, but the content of each monosaccharide residue was
different. Therefore, GPS-1 was identified as an RG-Ⅰ structure and contained a large
number of AG domains (the total Gal and Ara accounted for 76.85%). Mean while,
GPS-2 mainly contained the HG domain (GalA accounted for 64.23%). Yu et al. and
Lee et al . obtained RG -1 from white and red ginseng using the enzymatic method,
respectively, but these RG -1-containing acid polysaccharides differed in
monosaccharide composition and molecular weights, which might be due to different
extraction methods [26-27]. In addition, our previous study found that heat processing
can affect the monosaccharide composition and molecular we ight of ginseng pectin ,
which might be related to the difference in the structure of the polysaccharides [12].

3.2. Cytotoxicity of GPS-1 and GPS-2 on HepG2 cells
In this work, HepG2 cells were used as model cells with lipid metabolism
disorder in vitro. HepG2 cells were incubated with 25–800 μg/ml of GPS -1 and
Journal Pre-proof

Journal Pre-proof
15

GPS-2 for 24 h, and the survival rate of the cells were detect ed using the CCK8
method. As shown in Fig. 4, when the HepG2 cells were treated with GPS -1, cell
viability did not decrease even at the highest concentration (800 μg/ml). However, the
GPS-2 of 800 μg/ml had a slight effect on the survival of HepG2 cells. Therefore, in
accordance with the results, the administration of the polysaccharides was below 800
μg/ml.

3.3. Effect of GPS-1 and GPS-2 on HepG2 cellular TG and TC levels
To investigate the effect of the polysaccharides on oleic acid-induced lipid
accumulation in HepG2 cells, we determined the contents of TC and TG in the model
cells. As shown in Fig. 5, HepG2 cells were treated with oleic acid for 12 or 24 h. The
intracellular TG and TC contents increased significantly compared with those in the
normal group (p < 0.01). After 12 hours of culturing with GPS -1 and GPS -2, the
levels of T C and TG in GPS -1 and GPS -2 group were not significantly lower than
those in the model group , and the highest inhibition rates were less than 1 2% (TG)
and 10% (TC). However, after 24 h of administration, the content of TG and/or TC in
the cells of the GPS-1 treatment group decreased in a concentration -dependent
manner. When the concentration of GPS-1 was 400 μg/ml, the contents of TG and TC
decreased by 48.77% and 45. 51%, respectively . In comparison, GPS -2 could not
effectively reduce TC and TG levels in the tested concentration ranges, except for 200
μg/ml. The content of TG and TC in the GPS-2 treated group (200 μg/ml) decreased
by 9.63% and 2 5.34%, respectively . The se results show that GPS-1 was more
Journal Pre-proof

Journal Pre-proof
16

effective than GSP -2 in reducing lipid accumulation , which may be related to the
difference in physicochemical properties and structure. As a complex biomolecule, the
structure of polysaccharides is closely related to biological activity. The conformation,
molecular weight, substituted groups, side chains and degree of polymerisation might
be the structural basis and active centres required in exhibiting the biological actions
of polysaccharides [28]. According to the results, GPS-1 was composed of the RG-Ⅰ
domain with a large amount of the AG domain, and GPS-2 mainly contained HG. The
structural differences might be responsible for the different activities. Studies have
suggested that AG domain in polysaccharides play a major role in their biological
function. Lee et al. proved that AG content is positively correlated with the activity of
acid polysaccharides of red ginseng. Yao et al. also found that AG contributes to the
antioxidant activity of polysaccharide-isolated Saposhnikovia divaricate. In addition,
several AGs are considered effective in modulating the disorder of glucose and lipid
metabolism [29-32]. In this experiment, the structural difference of GPS -1 and GPS-2
might be the main reason for the different activity . GPS-1, with more AG domains,
might be the required structural basis for its hypoglycemic activities. In addition, the
molecular weight of the GPS -1 was 2.8 times that of GPS -2, which might be another
reason for the difference in the biological activity of these two polysaccharides. The
structure-activity relationships involved in reducing the lipid accumulation of GPS-1
needs an in-depth research.

3.4. Effect of GPS-1 and GPS-2 on lipid accumulation in HepG2 cells
Journal Pre-proof

Journal Pre-proof
17

Oil red O, a red fat -soluble dye that specifically binds to triglycerides in tissues
and cells and then stains the fat inside the cell s, was used to investigate the effect of
the polysaccharides on lipid accumulation in palmitate-induced cells.
As shown in Fig. 6A, after incubation with oleic acid for 24 h, many red lipid
droplets were observed in the cells, indicating the successful establishment of the lipid
accumulation cell model. After administration with GPS-1, the lipid accumulation of
HepG2 cells induced by oleic acid decreased to some extent . Compared with the
inhibitory effect on lipid accumulation in the negative control group, the effect in the
GPS-1 treated group could be observed significantly . With the increase in GPS-1
concentration, the red lipid droplets in HepG2 decreased gradually and became
smaller and lighter than before. The optimum effect was 400 μg/ml. However, GPS-2
had no obvious inhibitory effect on lipid accumulation within the detection doses.
The oil red O dye from lipid droplets can be dissolved by 60% isopropanol, and
the OD value, which reflects the triglyceride content indirectly, can be measured . In
this work, t he absorbance at 485 nm in the negative control group was significantly
higher than that in the control group (P<0.01). Compared with the negative control
group, the content of lipid droplets in HepG2 treated with 200 and 400 μg/ml GPS -1
decreased significantly (P<0.01), indicating that GPS-1 could better inhibit lipid
accumulation in vitro (Fig.6B). According to our previous study, GPS exhibits a
significant anti -diabetic effect , which is related to its antioxidant activity that
immuno-enhances and stimulates increased insulin secretion [11]. In the current study,
we also found that GPS-1 purified from GPS significantly inhibited lipid

accumulation in HepG2 cells, indicating that the anti -diabetic effect of GPS might be
related to its improvement of lipid metabolism disorders.

3.5. Effects of GP S-1 on phosphorylation of AMPK and ACC and SREBP -1c
expression

AMPK can maintain balance between cell energy supply and demand through
many links that affect cell material metabolism, which is called ‘energy receptor’ [33].
Recent studies have shown that AMPK occupies a central position in the regulation of
lipid metabolism. Therefore, we first invested the effect of GPS-1 on the expression of
AMPK. Oleic acid-induced HepG2 cells were treated with different concentrations of
GPS-1 to determine if GPS -1 affects lipid accumulation by activating AMPK. The
AMPK and phosphorylated AMPK (p-AMPK) protein expressions were evaluated. As
shown in Fig. 7, the protein expression of p-AMPK level in oleic acid-induced HepG2
cells w as significantly suppressed. By contrast , GPS-1 treatment at different
concentrations for 24 h significantly increase d the level of p-AMPK. Compared with
the negative group, GPS-1 treatment ( 200 and 400 μg/ml) could induce AMPK
phosphorylation. In addition, the p -AMPK level increased when the cells were
administrated with metformin for 24 h at 100 μg/ml. These results suggest that GPS-1
could activate AMPK.
SREBP-1c is a major nuclear transcription factor for the regulation of fat
metabolism and directly affects TG synthesis through regulating more than 30 lipid

metabolism-related proteins , such as acetyl-CoA carboxylase (ACC) , fatty acid
synthase (FAS) and Stearoy-CoA desaturase 1 (SCD1)[34-35]. Activated AMPK can
inhibit the transcription of SREBP -1c by directly phosphorylating SREBP -1c at Ser
372, which could down-regulate the expression of SREBP -1c and its downstream
target genes. SREBP-1c is acritical target for inhabitation of lipid accumulation [36].
Thus, activation of AMPK and inhibition of SREBP-1c is an important therapeutic
target for lipid metabolism disorder and type 2 diabetes [ 37-39]. In this work , a fter
incubation with 100 μM oleic acid for 24 h, the protein expression levels of total
SREBP-1c (125 kDa) and proteolytic SREBP -1c (68 kDa) increased significantly
compared with those in the normal group (Fig. 7). After administration with GSP -1
(100–200 μg/mL) and metformin (100 μg/mL), the total SREBP-1c protein expression
was suppressed significantly compared with that in the negative group. These results
reveal that GPS -1 treatment increased the phosphorylation of AMPK, which inhibit
the expression of SREBP-1c.
ACC, one of the SRPBP-1c’s target genes, is a rate-limiting enzyme that catalyzes
the first step reaction of fat acid synthesis and plays a key role fatty acid synthesis and
oxidation pathways [ 40]. According to the western blotting results, the protein
expression levels of p -ACC in model were decreased in model group comprised with
the normal group. When treated with GPS -1, the protein level s of p-ACC in HepG2
cells were increased. Compared with that of the negative group, GPS-1 at 200 and 400
μg/ml could significantly increase the expression of p -ACC (p<0.05 or p<0.01).
Studies have shown that some polysaccharides could inhibit the expression of

SREBP-1c to regulate the expression of ACC, and finally improved lipid metabolism
[41]. Thus, GPS-1 exerted a potent hypolipidemic effect through activation of the
AMPK, inhibition of SREBP-1c and inactivation of ACC.

4. Conclusion
GPS-1 and GPS-2 were obtained from the pectin of steamed ginseng , and their
fine structures were elucidated. GPS-1 and GPS-2 were composed of the same sugar
residues, namely, t-Araf, 5-Araf, 2, 4-Rhap, t-Galp, 4-GalAp, 4-Glcp, 4-Galp and 3,
6-Gal. However, they had different molar ratios. The m ethylation analysis showed
that GPS-1 mainly contained AG domains, and GPS-2 consisted primarily of the HG
domain. GPS-1 had a stronger effect on decreasing the TG and TC level s and lipid
accumulation compared with GPS-2. Moreover, GPS-I stimulated the protein
expression of p -AMPK, inhibited the expression of SREBP -1c and ACC and in the
oleic acid -induced HepG2 cells. These results reveal that GPS-1 exerts a potent
hypolipidemic effect through the activation of AMPK-related signalling pathways.
